title: KV-cache engineering
subtitle: The key-value cache is the largest thing on the card after the weights. I moved it to the host in ActiveKV, kept it hot in the Inference Fabric's broker, and in both cases measured the bus.

stats.label: worst error of the bus latency model against measurement, 32K to 262K tokens

lede: ActiveKV: stock serving keeps a request's whole key-value cache on the GPU, so a 32 GB card caps how much context it can hold. I made pinned host memory the owner of the cache and gave the GPU a bounded working set. The exact path re-reads every byte of history for every generated token, so I wrote the cost down as a latency model before changing anything. From then on, every design choice answered to that arithmetic. I treat the cache as a memory-hierarchy problem with a measurable cost on the bus. Each staged layer holds a lease.
quote: I count bytes before I optimise.
evidence: KV-cache offload for LLM inference: pinned host memory as owner of the cache and a leased, bounded GPU working set, with whole-layer staging bit-identical to fully resident attention.
Performance modelling: a bus latency model that predicted measured inter-token latency within 3.3% from 32K to 262K tokens, with a 262K-token context at a 22 GiB device peak.
Attention kernel engineering: exact log-sum-exp merging of tiled attention over exact and 8-bit pages, with a log-sum-exp output patched into the vendor's paged-decode kernel.
Latency engineering under concurrency: a hybrid tier at 190 ms per token against 335 ms exact at 128K, and about 8 GB of freed memory spent to cut latency from 274 ms to 141 ms.
author: Corey James
